name: Aaron Nakamura

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I work for the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, unions, AI companies, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal workday look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I play double bass in a small theatre band, record short parts and teach three older beginners. I have a music bachelor’s and plenty of working years, but I am an ordinary section player. I love the low note that holds a scene together; hauling the bass onto the last train is the part no audience sees.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How do those dates sit beside home bills?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 58, my partner works the grocery till and our children are grown. We rent and have about three weeks of expenses saved; music pay is low here and there are few other bands nearby. I use AI now and then to draft a rehearsal calendar, but I check the times with the stage manager before travelling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the theatre a faster call sheet is welcome if the bass player’s fee and last train are written down. I would still check the time with the stage manager.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Even if AI goes nowhere, our rent and the gap between shows stay. Three weeks saved would not cover a long run without dates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I would keep the paid theatre sets, three pupils and recordings, and ask for next run’s rehearsal and cancellation terms in writing. In the first plateau year I would request my actual pension estimate before naming a retirement date and save a quarter of cleared extra recording fees after rent, food and train fares toward one month of bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about ordinary rent and uneven dates already. The bass cannot be stored in a promise of next month’s work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you accept another distant show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if the written fee after the return train is worth the time and the last service runs. A show is not a gain if I pay to get home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you retire at 60?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have not seen a pension estimate. I would keep paid dates while my partner and I read the actual number.

I would check the **last train** and time with the stage manager.
think: Our **three-week reserve** cannot cover a long show gap.
The **rent** is due even if AI changes little.
do: Keep **theatre, pupils and recordings** with written rehearsal and cancellation terms.
Request **actual pension estimate**; save quarter of cleared extra recording fees after essentials toward one month.
feel: I feel **anxious** about current rent and uneven work.
S0.quote: A show is not a gain if I pay to get home.
fieldNote: His **thin reserve** and low, uneven theatre pay make a plateau anxious.
He requests an **actual pension estimate** instead of assuming a retirement date while rent remains due.

steps.text: Keep paid theatre, three pupils and recordings; request written fees and pension estimate

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the theatre which paid recording and rehearsal hours will remain. I would tell adult learners that a bass lesson needs a safe instrument and a paid teacher.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect generated bass tracks to take most short recording calls, about a third of my pay, and one rehearsal could go. Three weeks saved and variable grocery hours make that a serious rent problem.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would keep theatre dates and three pupils and get recording rates in writing. If two monthly recording calls disappear, I would offer a separate adult bass workshop only after a written room booking and seven deposits cover room hire, my teaching and preparation, a paid helper to move basses, safe instrument hire and train fares; I would replace an unsafe bass or defer and refund the whole group below seven safe paid places, and renew during disruption only if seven fees cover all wages and costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed about losing a large slice of income that pays rent, and I am awake at night counting the next dates. An adult bass workshop is a test only when seven people actually pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a paid helper?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two basses have to move without hurting anyone, and I cannot play and carry both. The helper’s setup hours belong in the fee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if one rental bass fails?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would find a safe replacement before the workshop. If seven safe paid places cannot remain, I would defer and refund the whole group, not take a short fee from the helper.

I would tell learners **safe basses** and paid teaching matter.
think: I expect **recording calls** worth a third of pay to vanish.

do: Keep **paid theatre and pupils** while seeking written recording rates.
Start **bass workshop** after two lost calls, written room and seven deposits covering room/own teaching/preparation/helper wages/safe hire/trains.
Replace **unsafe bass** or defer/refund whole group below seven safe places; renew only with all wages/costs covered.
feel: I feel **alarmed** about a large expected pay cut and rent.
S1.quote: An adult bass workshop is a test only when seven people actually pay.
fieldNote: The **seven-place floor** funds his own labour, helper wages, safe hired basses, written room and trains.
An **unsafe rental** needs replacement or whole-group deferral/refund below seven safe places.

steps.text: Keep paid theatre and three pupils; request written recording rates
Start bass workshop after two-call loss and written room; seven deposits cover room/own-teaching/prep/helper-wage/safe-hire/trains
Replace unsafe bass or defer/refund whole group below seven safe places; renew fully paid

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the theatre that 2028 thinking AGI could book and make bass tracks before robot players arrive around 2031. I would ask for signed live dates now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect short recording calls to end and paid rehearsals to shrink in 2028. Together those are more than a third of my low income. The rent has only three weeks of cover.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Before 2028 I would get signed theatre dates and keep three pupils. In the first year after 2028, if recordings end and rehearsals fall, I would apply for a posted paid theatre schedule-office role only if my music bachelor’s and years arranging calls meet its requirements, written net pay after train fares replaces lost fees and the last train works; I would keep paid band and pupils until a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed about a large cut in two years and it keeps me awake. I could apply for office work, but nearby paid openings are scarce.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you have the office experience?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have arranged rehearsal calls for my section, but I would read the actual posting. My music degree and that experience must be accepted, not assumed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would robots play bass in 2028?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The card puts capable robot players around 2031. Booking and recordings can reduce my pay in 2028, which is the first hit I would plan for.

say: I would separate **2028 thinking AGI** from robot bass players around 2031.
I would ask for **signed live dates** now.
think: I expect **recordings and rehearsals** to lose over a third of pay.
Our **three-week reserve** cannot bridge a long job search.
do: Keep **theatre and pupils** with signed dates before 2028 and until replacement offer.
Seek **posted schedule-office role** after recording/rehearsal loss; require accepted music bachelor’s/call experience, written replacement net after trains and last service.
feel: I feel **alarmed** about a large near-term income loss.
S2.quote: The rent has only three weeks of cover.
fieldNote: The **2028 threat** hits booking and tracks before robot bass playing around 2031.
The **office route** needs posted paid hours, accepted degree/call experience and written net after the train.

steps.text: Keep paid theatre and three pupils until signed replacement offer; request dates before 2028
Seek posted schedule-office role after losses; bachelor’s/call experience accepted, written replacement net after trains, last service

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the theatre that five years gives us time to ask what a live bass call pays. Thinking AGI is around 2031 and robot players around 2034 in this picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Recording work may fade, and there are few nearby stages. I would look at live-sound work, but a course certificate is useful only if an employer actually accepts it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would keep paid band and three pupils and check real posted theatre sound-assistant roles. If recordings and rehearsals fall, I would take a live-sound course only after a funded place and paid training hours are confirmed, a posting accepts the resulting certificate, and the timetable leaves my paid music hours and last train intact; in the first year after 2031 I would move only to that posted paid role if written net pay after travel replaces lost fees and transport works, keeping music until a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about recording income over the next few years. Five years gives me time to find a real course place and a job, but it does not pay next month’s rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if tuition is free but time is unpaid?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not take it. I need paid course hours without losing a paid rehearsal, or I would stay at the theatre.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you mix a show on your own after class?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. A technician would supervise my first sound checks until equipment and safety checks are signed off. A certificate alone does not make me safe at a crowded show.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my grown children that thinking AGI around 2036 and robot bass players around 2039 are separate dates. I would still ask what a real rehearsal pays today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 68 I may prefer fewer late shows, but I have no retirement date until I see the actual pension estimate. Rent and three weeks saved make the next few years risky even before AGI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I would keep paid theatre work and three pupils, request my actual pension estimate and save a quarter of cleared extra workshop surplus after my teaching/preparation, helper, room, safe hire, trains, rent and food toward one month. Over the decade I would run the separate workshop only after a written room and seven deposits cover those wages and costs, replacing unsafe basses or deferring and refunding the whole group below seven safe paid places; in the first year after 2036 I would renew only on the same full paid floor and keep theatre calls that still pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious because rent is exposed this year, not only in 2036. Ten years of warning does not add a week of savings by itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you borrow for more basses?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I would rent safe ones only against seven cleared fees and leave rent money alone. If a bass fails and I cannot replace it, the whole group is deferred and refunded below seven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you stop at 68?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No date is set. I would compare the real pension estimate with rent and the work I can still do.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 picture worries me most because recordings and rehearsals could take more than a third of my low pay. Signed theatre dates, a qualifying paid office vacancy and a written net offer after trains would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether the bass can reach the venue before counting the fee. A musician can earn a good rate on paper and lose it on the last train.

headlineQuote: A musician can earn a good rate on paper and lose it on the last train.
portrait: Aaron is an **experienced double-bassist** with a music bachelor’s, three pupils and low local pay.
He has **three weeks saved**, a grocery-working partner, grown children and rent.
He uses **AI occasionally** for draft calendars, checking times with the stage manager.
He considers a **funded sound course** only with paid time, recognized qualification and no lost gigs.
biggestWorry: The **2028 scenario** could cut more than a third of his low income before replacement work appears.
whatWouldHelp: He needs **signed theatre dates**, a qualifying paid office vacancy and written replacement net after trains.
